opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we spent a lot of time on early. At the end of the day, you have to pick some representation for the world, and that choice ends up shaping everything downstream: what the model can learn, how fast you can render, and what people can actually do with the output.

For us, the atomic unit has been Gaussian splats. You can think of a splat as a little fuzzy, semi-transparent blob in 3D space. Each one has a position, an orientation, a scale, a color, and an opacity. A scene is just a huge collection of them, often millions. When you render, you project all these blobs onto the image plane and blend them together.

There are a few reasons we like that. First, it's really expressive. Splats can capture fine detail, view-dependent effects, and messy real-world stuff like foliage or hair that's painful to get with clean polygon meshes. Second, it renders extremely fast. You can get real-time frame rates on a laptop or even in a browser on a phone, which matters a lot if you want people to actually walk around inside these worlds instead of just watching a video. And third, it's a fairly natural target for a neural network to produce. It's explicit 3D, so you get real geometric consistency. When you turn around, the thing behind you is still there. That's something you don't get for free from pure video generation.

That said, I don't think splats are the final answer for everything. They're great for appearance and for capturing what a scene looks like, but they're less natural for things like physics, collision, or editing individual objects. So we also think about exporting to other representations like meshes for collision, or eventually having more structured, object-level representations on top. I think the long-term picture is a layered one: some dense, high-fidelity representation for how the world looks, plus more semantic and structured layers for how the world behaves and how you interact with it.

But the core philosophy is that the world should really be 3D, not just a sequence of pixels that happens to look 3D. That's the bet we're making: spatial intelligence needs an actual spatial representation underneath it.

r001.rationale: It says fast rendering supports real-time walking around the worlds, but does not state that this enables precise camera control.

r002.rationale: It identifies Gaussian splats as the atomic unit, rather than saying individual splats are not a fundamental requirement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, the first question you have to answer when you're building a system that generates 3D worlds is: what is the atom? What's the thing you're actually producing at the end of the pipeline? And historically, in computer graphics, that answer was the triangle mesh. Everything downstream, every game engine, every renderer, every artist's workflow, is built around meshes with textures and materials. That's an enormously powerful representation, but it's also a really awkward thing to generate directly with a neural network. Meshes have this irregular, combinatorial structure, and the topology is discrete, so gradients don't flow nicely through the thing you'd actually want to optimize.

So a lot of my research career, going back to the NeRF era and even before, has been about asking whether there are alternative representations that sit closer to what the network wants to produce, while still being something you can render and interact with. For a while that was implicit neural fields, and then Gaussian splatting kind of changed the game because it gave you something explicit, something you can render extremely fast, that's still smooth and differentiable and friendly to learning. At World Labs we've leaned heavily into that family of representations. A splat-based world is essentially a big cloud of little primitives, each with position, shape, color, opacity, and the renderer just composites them. It turns out that's a really good target for a generative model, because the model doesn't have to reason about topology, it just has to put stuff in the right place in space.

But I'd actually push back on the framing a little bit, because I don't think the building block is really the primitive. The deeper building block is consistency. What makes something a world rather than a picture is that when you move your head, the thing you see changes in a way that respects a single underlying 3D reality. Objects occlude each other correctly, parallax works, you can walk behind something and it's still there. Video models have gotten astonishingly good at making frames that look right, but they're hallucinating that consistency frame by frame, and it tends to break down the moment you try to revisit a place. So for us the real atom is a persistent spatial structure that the model commits to, and then everything else, the rendering, the appearance, the ability to go explore, falls out of that commitment.

The other piece I'd mention is scale of context. A world isn't just one object on a turntable, it's a room, a street, a landscape, and the model has to understand how things relate across distances much larger than any individual primitive. So you need building blocks at multiple levels: the low-level primitives that get rendered, the mid-level notion of surfaces and objects, and the high-level layout and semantics of a scene. A lot of the interesting engineering is in figuring out how those levels talk to each other, and how you get a model to generate something coherent at all of them simultaneously rather than just nailing the local texture and getting the global structure wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says Gaussian splats can be rendered extremely fast, but does not connect real-time rendering to precise camera control.

r002.rationale: It says the primitive is not the deeper building block and identifies persistent spatial structure as the real atom, making individual Gaussian splats nonessential to the fundamental unit.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in terms of geometry, appearance, and behavior. Geometry is the structure of the world: where things are, how big they are, and how they relate to one another in space. Appearance is what those things look like—their materials, the lighting, and how your view changes as you move around. And behavior is what happens over time or when you interact with something.

The key is that these have to fit together into a coherent world. If you look at an object, turn away, and come back, you expect it to still be there. If you walk around it, you expect to see another side of the same object. So the fundamental thing we want is a persistent spatial representation that can support those different views and, ultimately, interactions.

r001.rationale: The response describes geometry, appearance, behavior, and persistent spatial representation, but does not mention Gaussian splats, real-time rendering, or precise camera control.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether individual Gaussian splats are required as the atomic units of the generated worlds.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental building block is a persistent, spatially consistent world. If you move the camera, you’re observing the same underlying scene from a new viewpoint. If you look away and come back, the things you saw should still be there.

That means thinking about geometry, appearance, and how those fit together in three dimensions. Where are the surfaces? What do they look like? What’s behind something that you can’t see yet? A model has to make those decisions in a way that stays coherent as you explore.

And there’s a useful distinction between the representation we use to render that world and the model that generates it. Ultimately, what we want is a world you can move around in and interact with, with a representation that supports those capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response describes persistent spatial consistency and moving the camera to a new viewpoint, but does not mention Gaussian splats or real-time rendering enabling precise camera control.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the rendering representation from the generating model, but does not state that individual Gaussian splats are not required as atomic units.
